question: A final-year student is about to perform a Pap smear. Which action is MOST important to ensure an adequate cellular sample from the transformation zone?

answers.text: Apply acetic acid to the cervix before inserting the spatula to improve cell pickup

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acetic acid is used in colposcopy and VIA, not in Pap smear sampling — it can alter cellular morphology and invalidate cytology results.

answers.text: Sample the squamocolumnar junction using the notched end of the Ayre spatula, rotating it 360°

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The squamocolumnar junction (SCJ) at the transformation zone is the site where dysplasia arises. Full 360° rotation with the notched end maximises TZ sampling and minimises false-negatives.

answers.text: Take the sample from the posterior fornix since pooled secretions concentrate shed cervical cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Posterior fornix sampling yields vaginal pool cells, not transformation zone cells — this is an inadequate technique and a known cause of false-negative Pap smears.

answers.text: Ask the patient to void 30 minutes before the procedure so that the cervix is better exposed by a full bladder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A full bladder does not expose the cervix; it can cause patient discomfort. The patient should ideally empty the bladder before a speculum examination.

overallFeedback.feedback: The transformation zone — specifically the squamocolumnar junction — is the site of origin for cervical dysplasia. Any technique that misses this area produces a false-negative result.
Well done. Sampling the squamocolumnar junction with a full 360° rotation is the cornerstone of adequate Pap smear technique.
